{{Quantum field theory}}
''' Tōichirō Kinoshita ''' ({{lang|ja|木下東一郎}}, '' Kinoshita Tōichirō ''; January 23, 1925 – March 23, 2023) was a Japanese-born American [[theoretical physicist]]. 

Kinoshita was born in [[Tokyo]] on January 23, 1925. He studied physics at the [[University of Tokyo]], earning his bachelor's degree in 1947 and then his PhD in 1952. Afterwards he spent two years as a postdoctoral researcher of the [[Institute for Advanced Study|Institute of Advanced Study]], Princeton, New Jersey, and then one year at [[Columbia University]]. His research interests included [[quantum field theory]], and the [[Standard Model]].<ref name="AIP">[https://history.aip.org/phn/11603021.html T. Kinoshita]. History. American Institute of Physics (AIP). Accessed October 4, 2018.</ref>

Kinoshita worked at the Newman Laboratory of Nuclear Studies at [[Cornell University]] from 1955. He was at first a research associate. In 1958 he became assistant professor, and in 1960 associate professor. He became a full professor in 1963, and in 1992 he was appointed Goldwin Smith professor. In 1995 he retired from Cornell as professor emeritus. In 1962–63 he was a Ford Fellow at [[CERN]]. He was a guest professor at the University of Tokyo, at CERN, at the national laboratory for high-energy physics [[KEK]] in Japan, and at [[RIKEN]] in Japan.<ref name="AIP"/><ref>{{cite web|title=Toichiro Kinoshita, Department of Physics|website=Cornell University (physics.cornell.edu)|url=https://physics.cornell.edu/toichiro-kinoshita|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161216195744/http://physics.cornell.edu/toichiro-kinoshita|url-status=dead|archive-date=December 16, 2016}}</ref>

Kinoshita was known for his extensive and detailed calculations of [[quantum electrodynamics]] (QED), the theory of the interaction of light and matter, on which physicist [[Abraham Pais]] called him the "expert among experts".<ref> Pais, A.1986. Inward Bound: Of Matter and Forces in the Physical World. Oxford: Oxford University Press, p. 466. </ref> QED is often described as the [[Precision_tests_of_QED|most accurate]] physical theory in existence. Among the best-known examples are Kinoshita's calculations of the 
[[Landé factor|anomalous magnetic moments]] of the [[electron]] and the [[muon]].

==Research==
Kinoshita worked on a range of topics in QED. While at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]] he calculated to high precision the ground state energy of Helium.<ref> T. Kinoshita, Phys. Rev. 105, 1490 (1957). </ref>
At Cornell, Kinoshita collaborated with [[Alberto Sirlin]] to calculate the radiative corrections to parity-nonconserving muon decay and β decay.<ref> T. Kinoshita and A. Sirlin, Phys. Rev. 113, 1652 (1959); T. Kinoshita and A. Sirlin, Phys. Rev. 107, 593 (1957).</ref>
He collaborated with [[Richard Feynman]] to calculate the radiative correction to the ratio of decay rates for a pion decaying to an electron over that for decaying to a muon, notated as Γ(π<sup>−</sup> → e<sup>−</sup>ν)/Γ(π<sup>−</sup> → μ<sup>−</sup>ν).<ref>
T. Kinoshita, Phys. Rev. Lett. 2, 477 (1959).</ref> In 1962 he showed that Feynman amplitudes in quantum electrodynamics remain finite in the limit of propagator masses vanishing, i.e., all infrared divergences cancel.<ref> T. Kinoshita, Jour. Math. Phys. 3, 650 (1962).</ref> This became known as the [[Kinoshita-Lee-Nauenberg theorem]]. In the 1970s he worked on [[quantum chromodynamics]] and [[quarkonium]] - spectroscopy with [[Estia Eichten]], [[Kenneth Lane (physicist)|Kenneth Lane]], [[Kurt Gottfried]], and [[Tung-Mow Yan]].

Kinoshita is best known for his calculations of the 
[[Landé factor|anomalous magnetic moments]] of the [[electron]] and [[muon]]. According to the Dirac theory,<ref> P. A. M. Dirac, Proc. Roy. Soc. Lond. A 117, 610 (1928). </ref> 
the magnetic moment of the electron should equal two. However, interactions of the electron with a magnetic field will deviate this value from two; the difference is referred to as the anomalous magnetic moment or simply “the anomaly” <math>a_e</math>. The value of <math>a_e</math> can be calculated as a perturbative expansion in powers of <math>\alpha / \pi</math>, where <math>\alpha = e^2 / (4\pi \varepsilon_0 \hslash c) \approx 1/137</math> is the [[fine structure constant]]. The lowest-order (“second-order”) term was calculated by [[Julian Schwinger]],<ref> J. S. Schwinger, Phys. Rev. 73, 416 (1948); J. Schwinger, Phys. Rev. 75, 898 (1949). </ref> and the next (fourth-order) term was calculated by Karplus and Kroll<ref> R. Karplus and N. M. Kroll, Phys. Rev. 77, 536 (1950) </ref> (with a sign error subsequently corrected<ref>A. Petermann, Helv. Phys. Acta 30, 407 (1957); C. M. Sommerfield, Phys. Rev. 107, 328 (1957). </ref>). The fourth-order term is obtained by evaluating seven distinct amplitudes or "[[Feynman diagrams]]." These calculations were all performed analytically, and their accuracy was limited only by the value of <math>\alpha</math>, which cannot be calculated from first principles and must be measured by experiment.

The sixth-order term consists of 72 Feynman diagrams, and Kinoshita evaluated these to high precision numerically using computers.<ref> P. Cvitanovic and T. Kinoshita, Phys. Rev. D 10, 4007 (1974). </ref> He revised this calculation in 1995<ref> T. Kinoshita, Phys. Rev. Lett. 75, 4728 (1995). </ref> using faster computers and higher-precision computational techniques. Working with his students, he subsequently calculated the eighth-order terms (891 Feynman diagrams)<ref> T. Kinoshita and M. Nio, Phys. Rev. D 73, 013003 (2006), hep-ph/0507249; T. Aoyama, M. Hayakawa, T. Kinoshita, and M. Nio, Nucl. Phys. B 740, 138 (2006), 
hep-ph/0512288. </ref> and, with great effort over several years, the tenth-order terms (12672 Feynman diagrams).<ref> T. Aoyama, M. Hayakawa, T. Kinoshita, and M. Nio, Phys. Rev. Lett. 109, 111808 (2012), arXiv:1205.5370; T. Aoyama, M. Hayakawa, T. Kinoshita, and M. Nio, Phys. Rev. D 91, 033006 (2015) [Erratum: Phys.Rev.D 96, 019901 (2017)], arXiv:1412.8284; T. Aoyama, T. Kinoshita, and M. Nio, Phys. Rev. D 97, 036001 (2018), arXiv:1712.06060; T. Aoyama, T. Kinoshita, and M. Nio, Atoms 7, 28 (2019). </ref>

In 2001, Kinoshita and a group in [[Marseille]] found a sign difference in their respective calculations of the π<sup>0</sup> pole contribution to the sixth-order light-by-light amplitude.<ref> M. Hayakawa and T. Kinoshita, Phys. Rev. D 57, 465 (1998) [Erratum: Phys.Rev.D 66, 019902 (2002)], hep-ph/9708227.</ref>  Kinoshita and his student M. Hayakawa ultimately traced this to an incorrect implementation of the antisymmetric [[Levi-Civita symbol|Levi-Civita tensor]] <math>\epsilon_{\alpha \beta \gamma \delta}</math> used in the computation code "Form"<ref> J. A. M. Vermaseren (2000), math-ph/0010025.</ref> that had been used.<ref> M. Hayakawa and T. Kinoshita (2001), hep-ph/0112102.</ref> It took a while to fix this software bug by the developers.<ref>[https://physicstoday.scitation.org/doi/full/10.1063/1.1461321 Schwartzschild, 2002]</ref>

==Personal life and death==
Kinoshita married Masako Matsuoka in 1951. He and his wife has three daughters. His wife died in 2022.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://ithacavoice.org/2022/08/obituary-masako-kinoshita/ | title=Obituary: Masako Kinoshita | date=8 August 2022 }}</ref>

Kinoshita died at his home in Amherst, Massachusetts, on March 23, 2023, at the age of 98.<ref>{{cite news |title=物理学者の木下東一郎・米コーネル大名誉教授が死去、９８歳…「最も高精度の理論計算値」 |url=https://www.yomiuri.co.jp/science/20230329-OYT1T50140/ |access-date=29 March 2023 |publisher=[[Yomiuri Shimbun]] |date=29 March 2023 |language=ja}}</ref> He was survived by daughters and sons-in-law Kay and Alan Schwartz, June and [[Tod Machover]], and Ray and [[Charles C. Mann (writer)|Charles C. Mann]], three sisters in Japan, and six grandchildren.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.ithacajournal.com/obituaries/bps138832 | title=Obituaries in Ithaca, NY &#124; Ithaca Journal | date=8 April 2023 }}</ref>

==Honors and awards==
In 1962–63 he was a [[Ford Foundation]] Fellow at [[CERN]]. In 1973–74 he was a [[Guggenheim Fellow]]. He was awarded the [[Sakurai Prize]] from the [[American Physical Society]] in 1990; the SUN-AMCO Medal from the International Union of Pure and Applied Science in 1998; the Gian Carlo Wick Gold Medal in 2010; and the Toray Science and Technology Prize in 2019. He was elected to the [[National Academy of Sciences]] in 1991.<ref name="AIP"/>
